cover.alt: A Muay Thai fighter throwing a high kick during a class at London Fight Factory

items.summary: A content refresh for London Fight Factory: a new portrait and a short video profile of every coach, a highlight film for the gym, and a fresh library of class photography.
items.overview: London Fight Factory is a martial arts gym just off Old Street, teaching Brazilian jiu jitsu, Muay Thai, boxing, wrestling, judo and MMA. We've photographed and filmed for them since 2019. By 2026 the gym's content had fallen behind the gym itself. The team had changed, the mats had changed, and someone thinking about joining had no easy way to see who'd actually be teaching them. So the brief was a foundation: introduce every coach properly, show what the gym feels like on a normal night, and give the marketing team a bank of new photographs to work from.
items.challenge: Seventeen people, most of whom don't spend their lives in front of a camera, filmed and photographed around a live timetable. Two mats run at once, classes don't stop for anyone, and the gym is dark, so the photographs come off the camera at high ISO. Each profile had to sound like the person, not a script: every sentence heard in full, captions that match exactly what was said, and b-roll of that coach actually coaching. The look of the photographs was agreed with the gym's marketing lead over several rounds, from a set of test grades to a clean, natural finish that keeps the character of the room, with the noise taken out properly rather than smoothed over.
delivered: Seventeen short video profiles, around 40 seconds each: the founder, the head BJJ coach, coaches for every discipline, and some long-standing members
Each profile captioned word for word, with a name card and the coach's role
A 90 second highlight film of the gym, in 16:9 for the website and 9:16 for social
A new portrait of every coach, all shot against the gym's cog wall so they read as one team
472 edited photographs from classes across July and August, every discipline covered
A colour grade built for the gym and signed off by their marketing lead, then applied across the whole set
Every photograph checked and levelled where the lines should be straight

items.overview: All Stars BJJ ran a full day at Crystal Palace National Sports Centre on Sunday 19 July 2026, with several mats going at once: kids divisions, adult gi and no-gi, women’s divisions, through to finals and podiums. A week later, Mat Masters 5 ran at Bromley High School. Both needed stills and video, and both had two audiences at the same time. cover.alt: A Super Efficient engineer lifting a manhole cover in a London back yard

items.summary: A single day filming one job in Enfield, cut into a longform YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels, with the channel set up so the work actually gets found.
items.overview: Super Efficient are London plumbers, gas engineers and drainage specialists, and almost all of their work comes from recommendation. That is a good problem to have and a fragile one to rely on. The brief was to turn the work they already do every day into something a stranger can watch, judge them on, and call them about, without adding a single day to their diary.
items.challenge: One shoot has to feed two completely different buyers. Homeowners and landlords want the satisfying clear and the honest explanation. Facilities managers and managing agents want the cost of not having a maintenance schedule. Those are different edits and different captions from the same footage, and getting that wrong wastes the whole day. items.summary: A case study film for the tethered version of NexBlue's Point 2, shot on a real swap-out install in Suffolk with the installer doing the talking.
items.overview: NexBlue added a tethered option to its Point 2 home charger and wanted to launch it on a real job rather than in a studio. The film spent a day in Shotley Gate, Suffolk, with Richard Gould of Essex Vehicle Charging, following the install from the van to the first charge and letting Richard explain why around 80% of his customers would rather have the cable fixed to the wall.
items.challenge: Installers trust other installers, not product copy. The film had to sound like a man on a driveway talking about a charger he fits every week, and one day on site had to supply a hero film, a separate product film, five verticals and the photography. The sun was hard and bright from start to finish, which is the least forgiving light there is for shooting a black charger on red brick. There was a curveball too. Richard normally works in his own company uniform, but on the day he chose to wear a NexBlue polo he'd been gifted, with a fleece over it that he took off as the day went on. It was only in the edit that we realised those shots couldn't go on wholesaler branch screens or social with the logo on show. Normally that's something you'd catch on set, but real sites don't always go to plan, so we found a way to fix it in post.

thumbs.heading: Taking the logo off the polo
thumbs.note: Comping, short for compositing, means laying a patch over part of the frame so something disappears without anyone noticing. Here that meant tracking the logo through 14 shots across the five verticals and every shot in the one minute cut, frame by frame, on the original 4K files. Each patch is clean shirt taken from the same shot, feathered so there's no edge, colour matched to the fabric around it and placed under the grade so it's graded with everything else. The NEXBLUE print on the back of his collar came out too, and every frame was checked at full size. A handful of shots couldn't be cleaned without it showing, so rather than ship a patch you could spot, we cut them and let the shots either side run on.

items.alt: The same shot of Richard playing twice side by side: on the left his navy polo shows the NexBlue logo, on the right the logo is gone and the shirt looks untouched as his hands move across it

items.summary: Team headshot sessions run on location for several companies, shot so every person looks like themselves while the set still reads as one company.
items.overview: A team page only works if it hangs together. The usual problem is that headshots get taken whenever somebody joins, by whoever is around, so a team page ends up a patchwork of phone photos, old crops and one very good picture from a wedding. These sessions were run on site, in one go, with the same setup for everyone.
items.challenge: Two things pull against each other. The set has to be consistent enough to sit in a grid without looking like a ransom note, and each person still has to look like themselves rather than processed. Most people also dislike being photographed, and you have a couple of minutes each before the next one is waiting.
delivered: On-site sessions, so nobody loses half a day travelling to a studio
The same lighting and backdrop for every person, so the set sits together in a grid
A few minutes each, run to a schedule the office can work around
Retouched files cut out and ready to drop straight onto a website or LinkedIn
Casual and behind the scenes frames from the same visit where the brief called for them

items.title: A WordPress catalogue under attack, rebuilt as a custom site

cover.alt: The TUK Ltd product catalogue, showing cabling categories and new arrivals

items.summary: A cabling manufacturer trading since 1984, running their trade catalogue on WordPress and being attacked through it. Rebuilt as a custom site of 371 pages, then moved onto infrastructure they own.
items.overview: TUK Ltd designs and manufactures voice and data copper cabling, selling to manufacturers, wholesalers and distributors rather than the public. The site is a working trade catalogue, so it carries the full product range, the specifications buyers check before ordering and the routes distributors use to get in touch. It has to be available, and it has to be quick to find things in.
items.challenge: The old site was built in WordPress and kept getting attacked. Every incident meant downtime on a catalogue that buyers and distributors depend on, and each fix was another patch on a platform with a very large surface to defend. It also sat on a previous supplier’s hosting, database, image storage and email, with their team holding administrator access, so nothing could be changed or moved without going through them.
delivered: A custom build replacing WordPress, leaving no third party plugin surface to attack
371 pages live, including 360 individual product pages generated from a single catalogue
Category browsing, featured products and new arrivals, each with its own route
Product search rewritten to match on every term rather than the whole query as one literal phrase, and no longer capped at ten results
Trade account registration with email verification, so pricing only appears once a buyer is signed in
A wishlist, so buyers can gather a parts list before they enquire
Separate request a quote and distributor enquiry routes, each reaching the right inbox
A distributor network page so buyers can find their nearest supplier
An admin area where the team publish their own content, with linking and video embedding built in
Migration onto the client’s own hosting, database, image storage and email, with no downtime
Repository made private, every legacy administrator and collaborator account removed, and every write route put behind a signed-in session
Pagination moved into the page address, so the browser back button returns buyers to where they were

outputs.label: Pages live, 360 of them product pages
Rebuilt off WordPress, no plugin surface to attack
Rows of live data migrated with no downtime
Results for a search that used to return nothing

items.title: A ten year old site rebuilt around the work they actually win

cover.alt: The rebuilt RH Ltd website

items.summary: A London electrical and building contractor with three distinct arms and a website that only really spoke about one of them.
items.overview: RH Ltd covers electrical work, developments and facilities maintenance for domestic and commercial clients across London, all NICEIC approved. The old site was a dark, single-column page built around a phone number and a contact form. It worked, but it didn’t carry ten years of completed projects, and it gave a facilities manager no reason to believe the firm handled anything beyond call-outs.
items.challenge: Three service lines, three different buyers, and one homepage. A homeowner wanting a rewire and a developer wanting a project managed need to see different things within about five seconds of landing.
delivered: A rebuilt site split clearly across Electricians, Developments and Facilities
A rotating hero showing finished work rather than stock interiors
Track record brought to the top: years trading, projects completed, services offered
Service cards that route each of the three audiences to the right page
Accreditation logos gathered in one place, NICEIC, TrustMark, Checkatrade, Nest Pro and the rest
Customer reviews pulled onto the homepage
A single clear call to action running through the page

outputs.label: Service lines given their own route through the site
Website designed and built
Rebuilt from a single dark page

items.title: Two brands for one wholesaler, TED EV and TED BMS

cover.alt: The TED EV website

items.summary: A family-run electrical wholesaler in North London with over fifty years in the trade. TED EV is an ecommerce site selling to registered installers, and TED BMS is a separate brand built to reach commercial building automation projects.
items.overview: TED supplies electricians, contractors and businesses across London and beyond. TED EV is the wholesale side, an ecommerce site with a strong EV charging range where installers order online and see trade pricing once they are registered. TED BMS is a separate brand for a different buyer entirely: the contractors, systems integrators, consultants and panel builders who specify and supply commercial building management systems.
items.challenge: The two audiences want opposite things. A TED EV buyer wants to know you stock the brand, see the trade price and get it in a basket today. A TED BMS buyer is working to a programme, needs supply that matches a specification, and is trying to stop chasing four different suppliers. Putting both on one site would have weakened each of them, so TED BMS was built as its own brand with its own goals.
delivered: A brand-led TED EV homepage putting the full manufacturer list above the fold
Click and collect, service and expertise stated as three plain promises
Trade registration as the primary call to action, with trade pricing shown once signed in
Full ecommerce on TED EV: product pages, basket and checkout, with new arrivals and featured ranges
Blog content written for installers, from toolkits to charger installation guidance
TED BMS built as a separate brand for commercial building automation work
Three clear ways in on TED BMS: trade account supply, commercial project support and technical product support
The four things that cost BMS projects time and margin named on the page, each answered directly
Product range laid out by category, from BMS and control cables through to control panel components
Audience routes for contractors, systems integrators, consultants, panel builders and facilities management
Credibility brought forward: over fifty years in electrical and trade supply, trade only, UK wide, specification aligned
Photography and video from our own shoots used throughout both sites
Social content produced alongside
An introduction film covering who they are, what they stock and where they are, for the site and their sales material

outputs.label: Sites, each built for a different buyer
Ways in on TED BMS, by what the buyer needs
Years in the trade, brought to the front of both
TED EV sells online, with trade pricing behind registration
